newsitem.title: USA: Just half of U.S. workers have pension plans.
newsitem.headline: Just half of U.S. workers have pension plans.

text.p: Will the U.S. "baby boom" generation go bust when it retires? Inadequate pensions, low savings and faltering Social Security have an increasing number of Americans worried.
Only half of working Americans are currently participating in some kind of private retirement plan, the Labor Department says. That percentage has been stagnant for 20 years.

"Our pension issues have been largely overlooked, yet they are profound," said Karen Ferguson, the director of the Pension Rights Center, a Washington-based public interest group that promotes the rights of workers and retirees.

Ferguson laments both the shortfall in pension coverage and the recent trend away from traditional employer-paid pensions toward something called a 401(k) plan, a savings strategy she disparagingly calls a "do-it-yourself" pension.

The U.S. pension patchwork is "widening the immense gap between the people who are wonderfully well off in retirement and sitting on their golf carts, and the people who can't pay the utility bills," Ferguson said.
Other analysts dispute that there is a pension crisis while agreeing retirement issues need much more attention.

"A number of people have gotten themselves all tied in knots about this. They are absolutely sure that the sky is falling," said Sylvester Schieber, an economist and vice president of Watson Wyatt Worldwide, a Washington consulting firm whose clients are primarily employers.

Schieber said that instead of being half-empty, the U.S. pension glass is actually two-thirds full. If one looks at Americans aged 45 to 59 and considers whether they or their spouses are participating in a pension plan, the coverage rate rises to 70 percent, he said.

Many of those not covered are employees of small businesses just trying to survive, or very young workers who may not care about a pension, said Lynn Dudley of the Association of Private Pension and Welfare Plans, which includes firms with a stake in operating pension plans.
"The last thing a fast food worker may want is to save for retirement. They may just want to get to college," she said.

Recent U.S. public debate has focused not on private pensions but on Social Security, the tax-supported government retirement program that provides the average full-career U.S. worker with 40 percent of what he or she earned while working.

Social Security is expected to be depleted in 2030 as the baby boomers -- the nearly 80 million Americans born between 1946 and 1964 -- retire. An advisory council could not decide how to save it, but council members suggested investing some of the funds in the stock market might help.

Could baby boomers compensate with private savings? Not at the present U.S. savings rates, one of the lowest of developed countries. In November, Americans saved 4.8 cents out of each dollar that they earned, the Commerce Department says.
Pension experts say these problems make it even more important to get U.S. pension policy right. That policy has changed dramatically with the times.
U.S. pensions started out a hundred years ago as rewards by big companies for long-term loyal service, but grew rapidly after World War II as unions bargained for them.

Until the 1980s, the traditional pension was a plan in which the employer paid out benefits depending on the employee's tenure and earnings. A federal agency created in 1974 still insures these old-style plans.

In 1981 new regulations were published saying employees could get tax breaks on earnings they put into company retirement plans. This launched the 401(k) system, named after a section of the tax code. But many companies require the employee to chip in before the employer matches the money.

The new system caught on quickly, while participation in traditional plans dropped by 30 percent in the last decade. But the new approach has problems, said David Certner, lobbyist at the American Association of Retired Persons.

"If you don't participate, you get nothing. It's okay for the better-off, but many lower-income people can't afford to contribute. Some people don't leave the money for retirement" (if they have a chance to cash it out), Certner said.

Some on Capitol Hill are trying to expand coverage with hybrids of the old and new pension styles. Last year New Mexico Senator Jeff Bingaman and Vermont Senator Jim Jeffords introduced legislation aimed at making it easier for small businesses to set up pension plans. They could do so by setting up a clearinghouse, and contributing at least one percent of salary. Employees could also make contributions.

"Baby boomers start turning 50 this year, one every nine seconds," Bingaman said as he announced the bill, which will be reintroduced this year. "By acting now ... we will help a graying nation avert serious problems in the future."
He said 71 percent of private sector workers in his state had no pension coverage.

If employer-paid pension coverage of full-time private sector workers does not at least double by the year 2015, Ferguson favors mandating a universal pension system. But she's apparently in the minority with that view.
No one expects such a proposal to come from the Clinton administration, which got badly burned when it proposed universal health coverage three years ago.
Employers would strongly resist a mandate, Dudley said.
"Employers are just not very paternalistic any more," she said. "Even IBM has said, 'we don't expect people to stay with us 30 years.'"
